meta.description: No film, no screenwriter. Hemingway wrote "men are dying this year who have never died before" in a 1930 letter — and credited a Key West boat captain.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Millions of people who have never died before will be killed'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a movie line. Hemingway wrote "men are dying this year who have never died before" in a 1930 letter — and said the joke wasn't his.

answer.label: Misquoted — Hemingway wrote ‘men are dying this year who have never died before’
answer.sourceLine: The documented line is from a 1930 letter Hemingway wrote to his friend Henry Strater: “He advised us all to be careful as men are dying this year who have never died before” — and the “he” is not Hemingway but his Key West fishing companion Edward ‘Bra’ Saunders, whom Hemingway credited every time he used it. The popular wording drifted twice over: first into the widely shared “People are dying who have never died before,” then into the apocalyptic “Millions of people who have never died before will be killed,” which no documented source contains.
answer.confidenceText: The joke is real and Hemingway wrote it down — but not in these words, and by his own account not first.

source.heading: What was actually written

docMeta.dd: Edward “Bra” Saunders, a Key West boat captain who introduced him to game fishing — a real person, not a character
“Millions of people who have never died before will be killed” — found in no film, transcript or text

source.excerpt: He advised us all to be careful as men are dying this year who have never died before.
trail: There is no film. Repeated searches for the popular wording as a screen line return no movie, screenplay, transcript or writer — only the fact-check cluster about the phrase’s political misattribution. Wikiquote’s Ernest Hemingway page ↗, checked in raw wikitext, does not list the line in any section, and Quote Investigator has no entry on it.

The earliest documented use is a letter, in 1930. AFP, reporting Sandra Spanier of the Hemingway Letters Project ↗, gives Hemingway’s sentence to Henry Strater in full: “He advised us all to be careful as men are dying this year who have never died before” — the words credited to boat captain Edward “Bra” Saunders.

Hemingway repeated it for a decade, and it outlived him in memoirs. FactCheck.org reports that biographer Jerry Rosco traced the detail to Mary Hemingway’s memoir “How It Was” ↗, by way of his life of Glenway Wescott — Hemingway, his widow wrote, would repeat the saying too often.

Then it drifted, twice. The circulating form shortened to “People are dying who have never died before” and was pinned on Trump in March 2020, Biden a week later ↗, and Greene in 2021. The escalation to millions killed appears to be a further embellishment with no documented source — an observation, not a sourced claim.
source.excerptNote: Hemingway is relaying a warning from his friend Bra Saunders, not making the observation himself — the “he” that opens the sentence is Saunders. Per Sandra Spanier, Hemingway used the line at least twice more, in 1939 and in late 1940 or early 1941, crediting Saunders each time.

source.rightsNote: US public domain turns on publication, not composition — and although Hemingway wrote this letter in 1930, private correspondence was not published in his lifetime. The letter reached print only in modern scholarly and selected editions well after 1930, so the pre-1931 public-domain cutoff does not reach it and the text remains in copyright to the Hemingway estate and its publishers. We have not independently verified which edition first printed this particular letter, so no edition, editor or page is asserted here.

author.name: Ernest Hemingway
author.kicker: The writer who wrote it down
author.heading: Ernest Hemingway
author.bio: Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist and journalist whose spare, declarative prose — in The Sun Also Rises, A Farewell to Arms and The Old Man and the Sea — reshaped twentieth-century fiction and won him the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature. He spent much of the 1930s in Key West, where the boat captains and fishing guides he drank and worked with supplied him with a steady stock of local turns of phrase. This particular joke was one of them: Hemingway repeated it for over a decade, in letters and in conversation, but he consistently presented it as someone else’s line rather than his own.

Exact edition and page of the letter not independently verified.

copyAttribution: "He advised us all to be careful as men are dying this year who have never died before." — Ernest Hemingway, letter to Henry Strater, 1930, quoting his friend Edward "Bra" Saunders. The popular version, "Millions of people who have never died before will be killed," is not what Hemingway wrote, and it is not from any film.

misattribution.heading: Who gets blamed for it
misattribution.intro: This line has spent a decade being put in the mouths of people who never said it. The pattern is always the same: the phrase reads as a malapropism, so it gets assigned to whichever public figure the sharer already considers a fool. It is also, less obviously, misattributed to Hemingway himself — he told everyone it wasn’t his.

items.why: A tweet dated 3/18/20 put “People are dying who have never died before” in Trump’s mouth during the early COVID-19 briefings. PolitiFact searched Google, Nexis and the Factba.se transcript archive ↗ and found no mention of it; FactCheck.org reached the same conclusion ↗.

items.scope: The follow-on version, one week later
items.why: By 24 March 2020 the same joke had been reassigned, as “People who have never died before are now dying from coronavirus.” PolitiFact rated it Pants on Fire ↗ — the clearest proof that the phrase attaches to a reputation, not to a speaker.

In June 2021 the line was attributed to the congresswoman. Lead Stories found no record of her saying it ↗ and traced the wording back to a letter Hemingway wrote to a friend in 1930, quoting another friend.

Hemingway wrote the line down, but presented it as Bra Saunders’s joke every time he used it — in 1930, again in 1939, and again in late 1940 or early 1941, according to Sandra Spanier of the Hemingway Letters Project ↗. PolitiFact puts it plainly: it “isn’t clear whether he was the one who coined it” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody famous said “Millions of people who have never died before will be killed.” A Key West boat captain named Bra Saunders made a joke; Hemingway liked it enough to put it in a 1930 letter to Henry Strater ↗, in these words: “He advised us all to be careful as men are dying this year who have never died before.”

context.heading: A fishing-dock joke that became a pandemic punchline
lead: The line began as gallows humour on a Key West dock. By Sandra Spanier’s account to AFP, Hemingway first put it on paper in a 1930 letter to the painter Henry Strater, relaying a warning from the boat captain Edward ‘Bra’ Saunders — and he used it at least twice more, in 1939 and in late 1940 or early 1941, crediting Saunders each time. Spanier notes the register changed as Hemingway aged: what started as a joke came to carry sorrow and regret. His fourth wife, Mary, recorded in her memoir that he would repeat the saying too often.

It reached most people ninety years later wearing someone else’s face. In March 2020, as COVID-19 briefings began, a tweet put “People are dying who have never died before” in Donald Trump’s mouth, dated 3/18/20. He never said it. Within a week the same words were being attributed to Joe Biden; by June 2021 to Marjorie Taylor Greene. The phrase had become a snowclone — a template that reads as a malapropism from whichever politician you already find ridiculous. The escalated form now circulating, with its millions killed, is the end point of that drift: a joke about mortality rewritten as a prophecy of slaughter.
detailsBody: The humour of the original depends entirely on its restraint. “Men are dying this year who have never died before” is a deadpan tautology — the absurdity sits quietly in the sentence and the reader finds it. “Millions of people who have never died before will be killed” forecloses the joke by shouting it: the scale (millions), the agency (killed) and the tense (will be) are all imported, and none of them are in the source.

The drift also flipped the phrase’s function. In Hemingway’s hands it was a private aside, passed between friends and eventually freighted with real grief. In its viral form it exists only to make a named public figure look stupid — which is why every fact-check of it has had to begin by establishing that the named figure never said it.
context.pull: Hemingway didn’t coin it either — he credited a Key West boat captain, every single time.
